People often have many unused messages in their monthly quota, so those could easily be used with no extra cost, or they value their privacy more than some money. Recipients could also be chosen randomly between other contacts (those not using TextSecure yet) to promote its use (default message) or a custom explanation by sender. Those messages would be in clear text. As this might be annoying it should be very limited (eg max 1 message to a single recipient per month, only during daytime...) to not be too intrusive spam. Dummy messages could contain other peer's phone numbers (random selection from those participating in dummy messaging, not just their contacts), never to be shown to user, just to send dummy messages to, to further mask the real social network. verdict.text:
One point needs flagging first. The brief says non-atomic requirements were excluded, but this run does not reflect that. It is the blind task over 50 source requirements, and 15 of them have more than one gold unit (tp+fn), expanding to 77 units. Either the filter was not applied to this run or the brief describes a different run. The units results below are real findings about non-atomic handling and should be read that way.

Track 1 is measurable here, but mostly for scope (76 missing) and condition (35). Actor, modal verb and action have 1, 1 and 4 genuinely missing cases, so their recall of 1.0 or 0.75 means nothing. The scope and condition "silent fills" also look partly like a parsing artifact rather than fabrication. In 4031-Signal#1, 6031-Signal#1 and 496-Signal#1 the LLM wrote no scope or condition clause at all, yet these are scored as "filled". If an omitted slot is being read as filled, the flag rates of 0.53 and 0.63 understate the model. Some fabrication does exist: in 1055-Signal#1 and #2 the model invented the scope "For each message draft".

The stronger pattern runs the opposite way to fabrication. The model refuses to supply the implied actor and modal verb, emitting `<MISSING_ACTOR> <MISSING_MODAL_VERB>` where all three annotators wrote "the App must". It does this in 36 of 71 implied actors and 47 of 76 implied modals. This conservatism produces the 49 "LLM incomplete, gold complete" verdicts and the overall verdict precision of 0.08. It is a calibration mismatch with the annotation convention, not hallucination.

Conversion similarity reaches about 77% of the human-human ceiling on sequence ratio (0.56 vs 0.72) and about 69% on Jaccard (0.38 vs 0.55). Much of that gap is mechanical. Humans use the fixed template "<MISSING_SCOPE>, <MISSING_CONDITION>, the App must", and the LLM drops the first two placeholders and replaces the third. The real semantic distance is probably smaller than the numbers suggest, but that is not established. The cosine entry (n=6, all zero) is broken and should be ignored.

Paska is largely measuring the same placeholder habit. The pass rate is 0.875 where the LLM produced a complete sentence and 0.08 where it did not.
